planting.note: Direct sow after soil is thoroughly warm and all frost danger has passed; the compact icebox-type vines fit well in smaller gardens.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Mickylee was released by the University of Florida and bred for early maturity and reliable resistance to fusarium wilt, a soil-borne disease that can devastate watermelon plantings in warm, humid growing regions where the fungus persists in the soil for years. The round, medium-small icebox-type fruit has sweet, crisp, deep red flesh with a thin rind, making a single melon a manageable size for a small household without leftovers going to waste. The compact vines and early ripening window make it a good choice for shorter growing seasons or for gardeners wanting an earlier harvest than larger, later-maturing watermelon varieties provide. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit stem browns and dries, and the ground spot beneath the melon turns from white to creamy yellow.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

common_name: King of Hearts Watermelon (AAS-Winning Seedless Hybrid)

planting.note: Start seed indoors and transplant after soil is thoroughly warm; as a seedless triploid, King of Hearts needs a nearby seeded watermelon variety planted for pollen to set fruit properly.

directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, planting a seeded watermelon variety nearby to supply the pollen this seedless triploid needs to set fruit. King of Hearts is an All-America Selections winning seedless hybrid producing large, oval, striped fruit with sweet, firm, deep red flesh and only soft, edible white seed traces rather than hard black seeds, a genuine convenience for fresh eating. The vigorous vine is a reliable, heavy producer when properly pollinated, and the flavor and texture rank among the better seedless hybrids available. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit stem browns and dries and the ground spot turns creamy yellow, since seedless watermelons give fewer reliable ripeness cues than seeded types and are easy to pick too early.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

common_name: Petite Treat Watermelon (AAS-Winning Personal-Size Seedless Melon)

planting.note: Start seed indoors and transplant after soil is thoroughly warm; as a seedless triploid, Petite Treat needs a nearby seeded watermelon variety planted for pollen to set fruit properly.

directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, planting a seeded watermelon variety nearby to supply pollen for this seedless triploid to set fruit. Petite Treat is an All-America Selections winner bred for genuinely personal-sized fruit, producing round melons small enough for one or two people to finish in a single sitting, with sweet, crisp, deep red, seedless flesh and a thin rind. The compact vine takes up less garden space than standard large-fruited watermelon varieties, and the smaller fruit size means a shorter time from pollination to harvest-ready ripeness. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit stem browns and dries and the ground spot beneath the fruit turns creamy yellow, the most reliable ripeness indicators for seedless types.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

planting.note: Direct sow after soil is thoroughly warm and all frost danger has passed.

directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Starbrite is a widely grown hybrid watermelon producing large, oblong fruit with the classic dark and light green striped rind most gardeners picture when they think of watermelon, and sweet, crisp, deep red flesh with a small, manageable seed cavity. The vigorous vine carries good resistance to fusarium wilt and anthracnose, two diseases that shorten productive vine life in warm, humid growing regions, helping the plant stay healthy and productive through a long summer season. As a dependable, well-proven hybrid with a long track record, it remains a solid standard choice for gardeners wanting a classic, reliable watermelon without the added complexity of seedless triploid pollination requirements. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit browns and the ground spot turns creamy yellow.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners
